planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; cutting back the oldest canes each late winter keeps the newest, most vividly bloomed stems on display.

directions: This western Chinese species is grown not for fruit but for its fern-like, deeply cut purplish-green foliage and arching canes coated in a ghostly white-grey waxy bloom that becomes most striking once the leaves drop in winter. Small purple-pink flowers appear in summer followed by inconsequential dark fruit. Cut a portion of the oldest canes to the ground each late winter to stimulate fresh growth, since young first-year canes carry the brightest, most intact white coating. Site in an open position where low winter light can catch the stems for maximum effect.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous, suckering species benefits from an annual hard cutback to maintain strong new whitewashed stems.

directions: Native to northern and central China, this vigorous, suckering bramble sends up tall, strongly arching canes that appear brilliantly whitewashed under a thick waxy bloom, an effect most dramatic in low winter sun against a dark backdrop. Small purplish flowers in summer give way to unremarkable black fruit that is rarely eaten. Because older canes lose their bright coating and foliage obscures it in the growing season, cut most stems to the base each late winter so fresh, fully whitened canes dominate the following winter display. It spreads readily by suckers, so site it where a thicket is welcome or control the colony's edges.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; allow ample room for its tall, stout canes and remove the oldest ones each winter to keep the display bright.

directions: A Himalayan and western Chinese species considered the showiest of the white-stemmed brambles, with stout, upright-to-arching canes coated in a thick, almost luminous white bloom and scattered with small prickles. Pairs of small white flowers in late spring give rise to golden-yellow, raspberry-like fruit that is edible but bland. Its larger stature and heavier stem coating than related ornamental brambles make it a strong focal point in a winter garden bed viewed against dark evergreens. Thin out second-year and older canes each winter so the newest, whitest growth remains the main feature.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this wild Chinese species prefers the same sharp drainage as its better-known relatives A. uniflora and A. schumannii.

directions: Collected and named for the Scottish plant hunter George Forrest, this deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub from Yunnan and Sichuan carries small, slender, white to pale-pink tubular flowers in summer, each backed by the persistent papery sepals typical of the genus that keep adding color after the petals drop. It shares the fine-textured, arching branching habit of its closer relatives A. uniflora and A. schumannii rather than the bulkier look of the common hybrid glossy abelia. Grow in sharply drained soil and give it a sheltered site at the colder end of its range, since it is less reliably hardy than some of its garden hybrid descendants. Light pruning after flowering keeps the habit tidy without sacrificing next year's bloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this white-flowered form is otherwise identical in habit and care to the pink-flowered species.

directions: This naturally occurring white-flowered form of beautybush trades the species' signature pale-to-rose pink for clean white, bell-shaped, yellow-throated flowers that cover the entire arching shrub in a dense late-spring display. Like the species it grows into a large, fountain-shaped, graceful shrub with peeling tan bark for winter interest, and bristly seed capsules that persist attractively after bloom. It is less commonly offered than the pink-flowered cultivars, so gardeners wanting a pure-white beautybush display should expect to source it from shrub specialists rather than general retail nurseries. Prune immediately after flowering, removing some of the oldest stems at the base to keep growth renewed.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
